title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: The doctor was not yet up. The footman said he had been up late and had given orders not to be woken, but would be up soon. The footman was busy cleaning the lamp-chimneys and seemed entirely absorbed in them. His concentration on his lamps, and his indifference to whatever Levin was going through, stunned Levin at first; but as soon as he thought it over he understood that no one knew or was obliged to know what he was feeling, and that it was therefore all the more important to act calmly, sensibly, and with resolve in order to break through this wall of indifference and get what he had come for.
"Don't rush, don't let anything slip," Levin told himself, feeling a steadily rising surge of physical energy and focus on everything he had to do.

Once he had confirmed that the doctor was not getting up, Levin ran through several plans and settled on this one: Kouzma would go fetch another doctor while he himself went to the chemist's for opium; and if, when he returned, the doctor had still not stirred, he would either tip the footman or — failing that — force his way in and wake the doctor by any means necessary.

At the chemist's, the lanky assistant was sealing up a packet of powders for a waiting coachman, and he refused Levin the opium with the same flat indifference the doctor's footman had shown for his lamps. Trying not to flare up or fall apart, Levin named the doctor and the midwife, explained what the opium was for, and tried to talk him round. The assistant called something in German through a partition, got an affirmative answer from the back, took out a bottle and a funnel, and deliberately poured the opium from a larger bottle into a small one, stuck on a label, and sealed it — over Levin's protests — and was about to wrap it as well. That was more than Levin could take; he snatched the bottle out of the man's hands and ran for the big glass doors. The doctor still was not up, and the footman, now busy laying out rugs, refused to wake him. Levin took out a ten-rouble note deliberately, and forcing himself to speak slowly — though wasting no time — handed it over and explained that Pyotr Dmitrievitch (what a great and weighty personage this Pyotr Dmitrievitch now seemed to Levin, when only yesterday the man had barely registered!) had promised to come at any hour, that he would certainly not be angry, and that he had to be woken at once.
The footman agreed, went upstairs, and showed Levin into the waiting room.
Through the door Levin could hear the doctor coughing, moving about, washing, saying something. Three minutes went by; to Levin it felt like more than an hour. He could not wait any longer.
"Pyotr Dmitrievitch, Pyotr Dmitrievitch!" he said pleadingly at the open door. "For God's sake, forgive me — see me as you are. It's been going on more than two hours already."
"One minute, one minute!" came the answer, and to Levin's astonishment he could hear that the doctor was smiling as he said it.
"Just for a second."
"One minute."
Two more minutes passed while the doctor pulled on his boots, and two more while he put on his coat and combed his hair.

"Pyotr Dmitrievitch!" Levin was beginning again in a despairing voice, just as the doctor walked in, dressed and ready. "These people have no conscience," Levin thought. "Combing his hair while we're dying!"
"Good morning!" said the doctor, shaking his hand and, with his calmness, almost seeming to tease him. "There's no rush. Well now?"
Doing his best to be precise, Levin began telling him every unnecessary detail about his wife's condition, breaking off again and again to beg the doctor to come with him at once.

"There's really no need to rush. You don't understand, you see. I'm sure I'm not needed yet — but I've promised, so if you like, I'll come. There's no hurry. Please, sit down. Won't you have some coffee?"
Levin stared at him as if asking whether he was being mocked; but the doctor had no thought of mocking him.

"I know, I know," said the doctor, smiling. "I'm a married man myself, and at moments like this we husbands deserve a great deal of sympathy. I have a patient whose husband always takes refuge in the stables when the time comes."
"But what do you think, Pyotr Dmitrievitch? Do you think it will go all right?"
"Everything points to a good outcome."
"So you'll come at once?" Levin said, glaring at the servant who was bringing in the coffee.
"In an hour."
"Oh, for God's sake!"
"Well — let me drink my coffee, at least."
The doctor started on his coffee. Both were silent.
"The Turks really are getting a beating, though. Did you see yesterday's telegrams?" the doctor said, chewing on a roll.
"No, I can't stand this!" Levin said, jumping up. "So you'll be with us in a quarter of an hour?"
"Half an hour."
"On your honor?"

When Levin got home, he pulled up at the same moment as the princess, and they went up to the bedroom door together. The princess had tears in her eyes and her hands were shaking. The moment she saw Levin she threw her arms around him and burst into tears.
"Well, my dear Lizaveta Petrovna?" she asked, gripping the hand of the midwife, who came out to meet them with a glowing, anxious face.
"She's coming along well," the midwife said. "Persuade her to lie down. She'll be more comfortable that way."

From the moment he had woken up and grasped what was happening, Levin had set his mind to bear the day resolutely, without thinking ahead or trying to anticipate anything, simply so as not to upset his wife — and instead to soothe her and keep her courage up. Without letting himself think about what was coming, or how it would end, and going by what he'd been told about how long such ordeals usually lasted, Levin had braced himself, in his imagination, to hold steady and keep a tight rein on himself for five hours; and it had seemed to him he could manage that. But when he came back from the doctor's and saw her suffering again, he began saying, more and more often, "Lord, have mercy on us, and help us!" He kept sighing, throwing his head back, and beginning to fear he couldn't bear it — that he was going to burst into tears or run from the room. That was the agony of it for him. And only one hour had passed.

But after that hour came another, and another, and another — the full five hours he had set as the outer limit of his endurance — and the situation was unchanged; and he was still bearing it, because there was nothing to do but bear it, every moment certain he had reached the very end of what he could take, and that his heart would crack from sympathy and pain.
And still the minutes and the hours kept going by, more hours after that, and his misery and dread only grew sharper and sharper.

All the ordinary conditions of life — the ones that ordinarily frame how you make sense of anything — had stopped existing for Levin. He lost all sense of time. Minutes — those minutes when she called for him and he held her damp hand that would clamp down on his with shocking force and then shove it away — felt like hours, and hours felt like minutes. He was startled when Lizaveta Petrovna asked him to light a candle behind a screen and he realized it was five in the afternoon. If she had told him it was ten in the morning, he would not have been any more surprised. Where he had been all this while, he knew about as much as he knew about the passage of time. He saw Kitty's swollen face — at moments bewildered and in agony, at moments smiling and trying to reassure him. He saw the old princess too, flushed and overwrought, her grey curls in disarray, forcing herself to swallow her tears, biting her lips; he saw Dolly, and the doctor smoking fat cigarettes, and Lizaveta Petrovna with her firm, resolute, reassuring face, and the old prince pacing the hall with a frown. But why they kept coming in and going out, and where they were, he did not know. The princess was with the doctor in the bedroom; then in the study, where a table set for dinner had appeared from nowhere; then she was gone and Dolly was there instead. Then Levin remembered he had been sent somewhere. Once he was sent to move a table and sofa. He had done it eagerly, thinking it had to be done for her sake, and only later realized it was his own bed he had been getting ready. Then he was sent to the study to ask the doctor something. The doctor had answered, and then started in on the irregularities in the municipal council. Then he had been sent to the bedroom to help the old princess move the icon in its silver and gold setting, and with the princess's old lady's maid he had climbed up on a shelf to reach it and broken the little lamp, and the old servant had tried to comfort him about the lamp and about his wife, and he had carried the icon and set it at Kitty's head, carefully tucking it in behind the pillow. But where and when and why any of this had happened he could not have said. He did not understand why the old princess took his hand and looked at him with pity and begged him not to torment himself, and why Dolly coaxed him into eating something and led him out of the room, and why even the doctor looked at him gravely and with sympathy and offered him a drop of something.

All he knew, all he felt, was that what was happening was what had happened nearly a year before in the country town's hotel, at the deathbed of his brother Nikolay. But that had been grief — this was joy. And yet that grief and this joy stood equally outside all the ordinary terms of life; they were a kind of opening in ordinary life through which one caught a glimpse of something sublime. And in the contemplation of that sublime something, the soul was lifted to heights it had never imagined, while reason limped behind, unable to keep up.

"Lord, have mercy on us, and help us!" he kept repeating to himself, feeling — despite his long, and as it had seemed complete, drift away from religion — that he was turning to God just as trustingly and simply as he had as a child and a very young man.

All through this he was in two distinct states of soul. One was when he was away from her — with the doctor, who kept smoking one fat cigarette after another and stubbing them out on the edge of an overflowing ashtray; with Dolly; and with the old prince, where the talk was about dinner, about politics, about Marya Petrovna's illness, and where Levin would suddenly forget for a minute what was going on and feel as though he had just woken from sleep. The other was at her bedside, where his heart felt as if it were breaking and somehow still did not break from the sympathy of suffering with her, and where he prayed to God without stopping. And every time some scream from the bedroom yanked him out of a moment of forgetting, he fell back into the same strange terror that had hit him in the first minute. Every time he heard a cry, he leapt up, ran to defend himself, remembered on the way that he wasn't to blame, and longed to defend her, to help her. But once he looked at her again, he saw again that help was impossible, and he was filled with terror and prayed, "Lord, have mercy on us, and help us!" And as time went on, both states grew more intense; the calmer he became away from her, completely forgetting her, the more unbearable her suffering and his helplessness in the face of it became. He would jump up, want to bolt — and run to her instead.

Sometimes, when she called for him again and again, he blamed her; but then, seeing her patient, smiling face and hearing the words, "I'm wearing you out," he turned and blamed God; and then, thinking of God, he immediately began begging God to forgive him and have mercy.
